name: Chase Dietary Method

lead: The Chase Dietary Method is a restrictive cleanse regimen devised by osteopathic physician Alice Chase (1898-1974). It centres on raw fruit and vegetables, vegetable juices, avoidance of sulfur-containing foods, and colon cleansing.

Its proponents framed it as removing retained waste to restore health. Any appearance benefit would be indirect and claimed, such as leanness or clearer skin from cleansing; it was proposed as a cancer treatment rather than a cosmetic one.

paras: Historical descriptions list fasting, vegetable juices such as celery and parsley, avoiding eggs, fish and meat, bed rest and enemas.
Medical experts describe the method as ineffective and potentially hazardous, and the American Cancer Society reviewed it as lacking evidence. Chase died of malnutrition in 1974.

angle.text: The method was never marketed primarily for looks. Cleanse-style regimens are sometimes pursued for leanness or clearer skin, which is an extension of the claimed detox effect.

lead: The Chase Dietary Method is an alternative regimen proposed by Alice Chase (1898-1974), an osteopathic physician influenced by John Henry Tilden [1]. It rests on the idea that retained waste in the body causes disease, so raw fruit and vegetables should be eaten to absorb it [1].

Practitioners historically combined fasting, vegetable juices, avoidance of sulfur-containing foods such as eggs, fish and meat, bed rest and enemas [1]. It was framed as a cancer approach rather than a looks one, and in appearance-oriented wellness talk it fits among cleanse and detox diets.

The American Cancer Society reviewed the method and reported no evidence of effectiveness against cancer, and medical experts describe it as ineffective and potentially hazardous [1][2]. Chase died of malnutrition in 1974 [1].

paras: Alice Chase, an osteopathic physician influenced by John Henry Tilden, sought to eliminate disease through diet [1].
Proponents held that unexcreted waste causes tumours and that raw fruit and vegetables absorb it, so they should be eaten daily [1].

A 1969 article in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians covered the method [2]. The American Cancer Society reported no evidence that it works, and US government reports in 1980 and 1984 listed it among unproven methods [1].
Experts describe the regimen as potentially hazardous, citing prolonged fasting and enemas, and Chase died from malnutrition [1].
